Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys Written by Non-SSH Tooling (Symlink Repo Payload)
id: 5c2e6b1a-9f3d-4a77-8b0e-2d1c6f9a4e21
description: Detects creation or modification of a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by a process that is not legitimate SSH provisioning tooling, consistent with a symlink committed to a cloned git repository resolving to authorized_keys and being written through by a build script, editor, or AI coding agent.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/symlinks-are-still-scary/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sshd'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '/ssh-copy-id'
      - '/cloud-init'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/salt-minion'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* AND (*">>"* OR *tee* OR *">"*)) -@process.executable.path:(*/sshd OR */ssh-keygen OR */ssh-copy-id OR */cloud-init)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(sshd|ssh-keygen|ssh-copy-id|cloud-init)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","git-remote-https","git-remote-https.exe","bash","sh","dash")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or FolderPath has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git","bash","sh","dash")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or ActingProcessName has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 9090
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc

// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 9090
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.

| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-i"

| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling

  • Backup/sync tooling restoring the Joro plugin directory

Nuclio CronJob curl shell-injection reading Kubernetes serviceaccount token AIExploitation High
Hunts a /bin/sh -c curl invocation (as built by the Nuclio controller for cron triggers) whose command line both reads the pod serviceaccount token and contains shell metacharacters, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-52831 header-key/body command injection. Article-specific because it pins on the exact curl --header shape plus the /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token read shown in the PoC. Rationale: Anchors on the exact PoC artefacts: a curl --header command line (the controller's generated sink) that also reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, plus shell metacharacters ($(, ;, &&) that only appear when Path-A/Path-B injection breaks the quoting context.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running kubectl exec into a pod and using curl -H with the serviceaccount token to test the Kubernetes API
  • Legitimate in-cluster script that curls the API server with a custom header whose value contains '; charset=utf-8'
  • CIS-benchmark / security scanner tooling that reads the serviceaccount token path
  • CI/CD sidecar that reads the token and curls an internal admission endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine contains "; charset=" or ProcessCommandLine contains ";q=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "kubectl")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and confirm the injected fragment (text after the closing quote of --header, or a $(...) in the echoed body); map the host/pod to the owning NuclioFunction and cron trigger. 2) Contain: suspend/delete the offending CronJob (kubectl delete cronjob), delete the NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod serviceaccount token / bound token if it was read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs in the nuclio namespace lacking ownerReferences, review other functions' cron trigger event.headers/event.body for metacharacters, and pivot on outbound connections from the same pod (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nuclio CronJob curl shell-injection reading Kubernetes serviceaccount token
id: 6f3a1c2e-8b4d-4e9a-9c1f-2a7b5d3e4f10
status: experimental
description: Detects a shell/curl process that reads the Kubernetes serviceaccount token inside a curl --header command line containing shell metacharacters, indicating exploitation of Nuclio CVE-2026-52831 cron-trigger header/body command injection.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - 'curl'

            - ';'

| regex("serviceaccount/token", field=CommandLine)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

Egress from Nuclio CronJob curl process reading serviceaccount token to public IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a curl process that read the serviceaccount token (the injected command) with an outbound connection to a non-private IP within a short window — the token/secret exfiltration step of CVE-2026-52831 RCE. Multi-stage correlation on the same host/pod. Rationale: Ties the injected token-reading curl (from UC1) to a public egress within 5 minutes — the exfiltration shape of the RCE. Uses the exact token path and curl process; RFC1918 exclusion isolates external destinations. CIM Network_Traffic field names may need site-local mapping. Empty CloudWatch/Sigma (multi-stage, non-AWS).
ATT&CKT1020 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Function legitimately curls an external webhook/API as its designed behaviour
  • Cron trigger intentionally targeting a public endpoint
  • Egress through a NAT/CDN/proxy destination that looks public
  • Outbound telemetry from a sidecar that also happens to read the token
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith ".svc.cluster.local" or RemoteIP startswith "100.64.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the same host/pod both read the serviceaccount token and made the external connection; resolve the destination IP/URL and check reputation. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, kill the CronJob/pod, and rotate the serviceaccount token and any secrets the pod could reach. 3) Hunt: pull all destinations contacted by curl processes on nuclio pods, look for repeated beaconing to the same external IP, and cross-reference UC4 for downstream API abuse with the stolen token.
let TokenReads = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
    | project TokenReadTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName == "curl"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner TokenReads on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (TokenReadTime .. TokenReadTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TokenReads = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
    | project TokenReadTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and DstIpAddr !startswith "127."
| join kind=inner TokenReads on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (TokenReadTime .. TokenReadTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 exfil to Paysafe-stealer ngrok endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Install of fake Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller npm & PyPI credential-stealer packages AIInstallation High
Hunts developer/CI machines running npm or pip against the 17 named malicious payment-SDK packages (paysafe-*, skrill*, neteller) that impersonate legitimate Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller SDKs and steal API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens. Article-specific because it keys on the exact package names published in this campaign, not generic dependency installs. Rationale: Uses the 17 exact package names Socket enumerated (paysafe-checkout, paysafe-vault, skrill-sdk, neteller, etc.) scoped to the actual package-manager binaries — high fidelity because these package names have no legitimate publisher and installation is the campaign's install step. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox to reproduce the campaign
  • An internal private-registry package that legitimately contains the substring 'skrill' or 'paysafe' in its name
  • A blue-team engineer running an IOC-validation install against a proxy that blocks the fetch
  • A dependency-audit tool that references the package names in a lockfile scan (not an actual install)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--registry=https://your-internal-registry" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the exact package + version installed (npm 1.0.0-1.0.3 or PyPI 1.0.0 are the malicious ranges) and identify the machine/CI runner and user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate ALL secrets present on that machine — Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens — per Socket's guidance. Deny the package names at the registry proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Search dependency trees org-wide for any of the 17 names, grep CI logs for PAYSAFE_API_KEY appearing alongside these package names, and pivot to UC2 to check for outbound exfil to the ngrok C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add"," i ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm","node.exe","pip","python","yarn","pnpm")
| where CommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install","add")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 exfil to Paysafe-stealer ngrok endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the campaign's exfiltration endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev, the C2 the fake payment SDKs POST stolen credentials/tokens to. Article-specific because it keys on the single confirmed IOC domain from this campaign rather than the whole ngrok TLD. Rationale: Keys on the single confirmed IOC domain (caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev) from the article — a direct match is nearly always malicious since it is the stealer's dedicated exfil endpoint, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst or threat-intel researcher deliberately resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • A DNS sinkhole/RPZ that logs the query before blocking it (query still appears in DNS telemetry)
  • Passive DNS collectors or scanning tools crawling the ngrok subdomain
  • The ngrok free subdomain being recycled to a benign tunnel by a different user after takedown
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the initiating process — correlate the connecting process (Node/Python) with UC1 to confirm one of the 17 malicious packages ran on this machine. Step 2 (contain): Block caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat all secrets on it as compromised — rotate Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep proxy/DNS logs org-wide for the same domain over 30d, review AWS CloudTrail for any use of exfiltrated AWS keys from unfamiliar IPs, and check GitHub/npm audit logs for token misuse.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Spear-phish to researcher followed by campaign C2 beacon · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2024-42009 Roundcube XSS payload load in webmail HTTP logs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] IceCube Roundcube stealer payload by SHA256 (a02f124c...) · [LLM] SquareShell PHP webshell drop in Roundcube web root (CVE-2025-49113) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UNK_MassTraction C2 egress to sslip.io / VPS IPs (IceCube/VShell) · [LLM] VShell in-memory loader: mail-server shell fetching campaign C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
UNK_MassTraction C2 egress to sslip.io / VPS IPs (IceCube/VShell) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host beaconing to the campaign's hard-coded command-and-control infrastructure — VPS IPs 45.150.109.151, 194.213.18.133, 45.86.229.111 and their sslip.io wildcard-DNS aliases used to stage IceCube and load VShell. Article-specific because these exact IOCs are only meaningful for this Proofpoint-tracked cluster. Rationale: Uses the three campaign VPS IPs and both sslip.io C2 aliases named as pre-extracted IOCs; these are only meaningful for UNK_MassTraction, so any hit is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher / sandbox detonating the sample and reaching the C2
  • Security scanner probing the sslip.io host range
  • Shared VPS IP later re-leased to a benign tenant (sslip.io wildcard reuse)
  • Internal proxy that logs the destination on behalf of a blocked connection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host/user initiated the connection and whether it is a Roundcube/mail server or a webmail-user endpoint; pull the initiating process. 2) Contain: block the three IPs and *.sslip.io aliases at perimeter, isolate the host, and force-reset credentials for any account that authenticated through the affected Roundcube instance. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for SquareShell .php drops, curl/wget-to-shell VShell loaders, and the IceCube hash a02f124c...; sweep other mail servers for the same egress.

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Alerts on the presence or execution of the specific IceCube payload hash reported for this campaign. Because it is a single known-bad SHA256, any observation is a confirmed campaign artifact rather than a behavioural heuristic. Rationale: Direct match on the single SHA256 IOC (a02f124c...) named in the article for IceCube; zero ambiguity, confirmed campaign artifact.
ATT&CKT1539 T1111
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst copying the sample onto a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR quarantine/restore cycle re-touching the file
  • Threat-intel feed sync writing the sample into a detonation share
  • Backup agent hashing an already-quarantined artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path/host and whether the process actually executed vs. was merely written; check parent process. 2) Contain: quarantine the hash org-wide, isolate the host, and invalidate session cookies + reset passwords/2FA for Roundcube users on that server (IceCube harvests cookies and 2FA). 3) Hunt: look for the C2 IOCs, SquareShell webshells, and VShell loaders on the same host and across the Roundcube fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SquareShell PHP webshell drop in Roundcube web root (CVE-2025-49113) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a PHP file written into a Roundcube document root or temp directory by the webserver/PHP runtime — the SquareShell webshell IceCube installs after exploiting the CVE-2025-49113 deserialization flaw. Article-specific to the Roundcube post-exploitation write. Rationale: Article states IceCube exploits CVE-2025-49113 to install SquareShell (a PHP webshell with RCE); this pivots on a PHP file being written into Roundcube paths by the web runtime — the concrete install action.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Roundcube upgrade / plugin install writing .php files
  • Composer/pear dependency deployment into web root
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) pushing PHP templates
  • Roundcube cache/temp writes that legitimately land in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","pear","apt","yum","dpkg") or FolderPath has "/vendor/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written .php for command-exec functions (system, exec, shell_exec, passthru, eval, base64_decode) and check whether it sits outside the packaged Roundcube file set. 2) Contain: pull the file, snapshot the host, and block inbound POST/PUT to the suspect path at the WAF; if RCE confirmed, isolate the mail server. 3) Hunt: correlate the write time with CVE-2025-49113 deserialization errors in PHP logs and with subsequent curl/wget VShell loaders and C2 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FolderPath has_any ("roundcube","/var/www","/usr/share/roundcube","/tmp/","/var/tmp")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "php"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("roundcube","/var/www","/usr/share/roundcube","/tmp/","/var/tmp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VShell in-memory loader: mail-server shell fetching campaign C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects a Roundcube/mail-server process spawning curl/wget or a shell that references the campaign C2 hosts to pull the shell script that loads VShell directly in memory. Grounded in the article's fallback chain when SquareShell install fails. Rationale: Article: on SquareShell failure the malware 'downloads a shell script that loads another payload, VShell, directly in memory'; this ties the download utility to the exact C2 IOCs for a high-fidelity, low-FP alert.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually curling from a host that happens to share the sslip.io wildcard base (rare)
  • Monitoring script referencing one of the IPs in an allow/deny test
  • Security team reproducing the loader in a lab
Suppression filter
| where AccountName != "root" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the parent (php/apache) — a webserver parent spawning curl-to-C2 is confirmation. 2) Contain: isolate the mail server, kill the process tree, and block the C2 IPs/sslip.io; snapshot memory to recover the in-memory VShell. 3) Hunt: enumerate listening ports / SOCKS / port-forwarding VShell may have set up, review outbound tunneling, and check other Roundcube hosts for the same loader pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","sh","bash")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111","sslip.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111","sslip.io")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2024-42009 Roundcube XSS payload load in webmail HTTP logs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Roundcube message-view HTTP requests carrying XSS payload markers or referencing the campaign C2 hosts — the CVE-2024-42009 stored-XSS that executes JavaScript in the victim's browser to load IceCube. Article-specific via Roundcube endpoints plus the campaign C2 aliases. Rationale: Article: opening the email 'triggers exploitation of a cross-site scripting flaw tracked as CVE-2024-42009, which executes JavaScript... loading a payload called IceCube'; pivots on Roundcube mail-view endpoints plus XSS markers and the campaign C2 aliases.
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) fuzzing Roundcube with XSS payloads
  • Legitimate email whose subject/body legitimately contains the string 'onerror' or 'javascript:'
  • Penetration test of the webmail instance
  • URL-encoded content in a benign forwarded message triggering %3Cscript match
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","sqlmap","ZAP","Nikto","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and target Roundcube host; confirm Roundcube version is unpatched for CVE-2024-42009 and inspect the request/referer for the C2 alias. 2) Contain: patch/virtual-patch the webmail, block the source and C2 hosts, and expire sessions for users who viewed the crafted message. 3) Hunt: correlate to browser fetches of the sslip.io aliases (endpoint side), IceCube hash presence, and any CVE-2025-49113 follow-on webshell activity.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("45.150.109.151.sslip.io","194.213.18.133.sslip.io")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spear-phish to researcher followed by campaign C2 beacon AIDelivery Medium
Correlates an inbound delivered email to a recipient with that same user's device connecting to the UNK_MassTraction C2 within 24h — tying the academic-researcher spear-phish to the campaign infrastructure. Article-specific via the C2 IOCs anchoring an otherwise generic lure. Rationale: Article: attack 'begins with a malicious email sent from compromised accounts or spoofed domains' targeting researchers; the generic lure is anchored to the campaign by correlating the recipient to a subsequent connection to the confirmed C2 IPs/aliases.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher independently browsing to a benign host that later re-uses the sslip.io wildcard IP
  • Shared/kiosk device where the beaconing user differs from the email recipient
  • Threat-intel analyst who both received a sample email and detonated it
  • Email recipient whose UPN maps to multiple devices, inflating the join
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the correlated email (sender, subject, headers/SPF-DKIM-DMARC) and the beaconing process on the recipient's device to confirm the chain. 2) Contain: quarantine the message org-wide, block sender infrastructure and the C2, isolate the device, and reset the user's Roundcube + corporate credentials and 2FA. 3) Hunt: search other researcher/faculty mailboxes for the same sender or lure and sweep for IceCube hash, SquareShell, and VShell loaders.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Sophos looked at a week of its own endpoint data and found that AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are setting off detection rules written to catch human intruders. The agents are not malicious. They just do a lot of things that, to a behavioral engine, look exactly like an attack. Decrypting browser credentials, listing what sits in Windows' credential store,

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attacke
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) · [LLM] Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact PowerShell one-liner GStack's /browse skill runs under Claude Code/Cursor to unlock Chromium credential data: Add-Type System.Security then ProtectedData::Unprotect on a base64 blob. Detects browser-credential decryption regardless of whether an AI agent or an attacker drove it, while surfacing the agent parent for triage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim GStack /browse command signature from the Sophos blog (ProtectedData::Unprotect + FromBase64String under powershell), which is the highest-fidelity string in the article; the AgentLineage tag distinguishes benign agent automation from real theft without dropping either. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's Claude Code running GStack /browse for legitimate browser automation
  • Password managers or browser-profile migration utilities that legitimately DPAPI-decrypt saved logins
  • Authorized red-team/pentest tooling exercising browser credential extraction
  • Security research or QA reproducing the Sophos finding
  • Backup/sync tooling re-protecting DPAPI blobs on the same user context
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName — if the parent is claude.exe/cursor.exe/codex it is likely benign agent automation; confirm the logged-on user actually runs a coding agent. 2) Contain: if the parent is NOT a known agent (real theft), isolate the host and force-reset the browser-stored credentials and any SSO sessions decrypted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for cmdkey /list, certutil/bitsadmin downloads, and startup-folder writes within the same session to separate agent noise from an intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Unprotect"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData" and CommandLine has "Unprotect" and CommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPAPI Browser Credential Decryption via PowerShell (GStack browse skill)
id: 6f1d2a94-8c3b-4a11-9e0f-7d2c5b4a1e33
description: Detects the GStack /browse skill's PowerShell that calls DPAPI ProtectedData.Unprotect on a base64 blob to decrypt Chromium browser credentials, observed running under Claude Code/Cursor and equally used for real browser-credential theft.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData'
      - 'Unprotect'
      - 'FromBase64String'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate GStack /browse browser automation by a developer's Claude Code
  - Password-manager or profile-migration tooling that decrypts DPAPI blobs
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*ProtectedData* AND *Unprotect* AND *FromBase64String*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/System\.Security\.Cryptography\.ProtectedData/i
| CommandLine=/Unprotect/i
| CommandLine=/FromBase64String/i
| agent := if(ParentBaseFileName=/(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe/i, "ai-agent", "other")
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, agent, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts cmdkey.exe /list — Claude Code was observed enumerating everything Windows Credential Manager holds. Rare in normal user space; the AI-agent parent lineage is surfaced to separate benign agent recon from an attacker's credential survey. Rationale: cmdkey.exe /list is the literal command Sophos attributed to Claude Code enumerating Credential Manager; it is uncommon enough in user space to hunt broadly while tagging agent lineage for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin auditing saved RDP / network credentials with cmdkey /list
  • Logon or provisioning scripts that inventory stored credentials
  • MDM/endpoint-management agents enumerating credential entries
  • A developer's coding agent legitimately checking cached credentials before an automation task
  • IT troubleshooting of Credential Manager / SSO issues
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain — a claude.exe/cursor.exe ancestor plus a developer user strongly implies benign agent recon; an interactive shell under a service or unexpected user warrants escalation. 2) Contain: if paired with credential decryption or exfil, isolate the host and rotate any credentials visible in Credential Manager for that user. 3) Hunt: search the same host/session for DPAPI browser decrypt (UC1), LOLBin downloads, and outbound connections to determine if enumeration led to use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "cmdkey.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/list"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmdkey.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/list"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Credential Manager Enumeration via cmdkey /list
id: 2a7c9e40-1b6d-4f28-8c11-3e9a5d7b4c20
description: Detects cmdkey.exe /list enumerating stored Windows Credential Manager entries, observed under Claude Code and used by attackers for credential discovery.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
